newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African offshore oilfield seen on stream in May.
newsitem.headline: S.African offshore oilfield seen on stream in May.

text.p: Energy Africa said it expected South Africa's first offshore oilfield to go on stream in May, boosting its production by about 3,000 barrels per day, managing director John Bentley said on Wednesday.

Briefing the media about the group's results for the six months to February 28, Bentley said the commissioning of the Oribi oilfield, which had been due to go on stream at the beginning of the year, had been delayed by bad weather.
Energy Africa has a 20 percent interest in the oilfield, with the rest held by state-owned exploration company Soekor.
"Forty days of the delay has been due specifically to the weather, but we do expect a further increase in our production levels once that field comes into production," Bentley said.
Energy Africa's working interest share of production during the six months was 1.8 million barrels of oil and condensate and 24,000 barrels of liquid petroleum gas.
This worked out to an average of 10,200 barrels per day (bpd) of liquids compared with 6,600 bpd in the same period last year.
The increase was mainly due to improved production from the Alba oilfield in the North Sea and a full six months' production from the Nkossa oilfield off Congo.
Bentley said that the exceptionally high oil prices over the last six months were unlikely to be repeated in the second half.
He added that the high prices had left most oil companies "with a lot of cash and that is driving more competition on the exploration side".
"It is pushing rig rates up and it is making it more difficult to get hold of rigs and we are seeing this in some of our exploration, which is now being delayed a little bit."
Energy Africa's cashflow from operations rose 136 percent to 98.2 million rand in the six months, while turnover rose to 149.4 million rand from 69.7 million rand.
High oil prices had also made it very dificult to do asset trades because of uncertainty about future price trends.
"So we have not been able to make any of the acquisitions that we would have liked to have during this period. Other than in the North Sea...there have been very few asset trades in Africa," he said.
"However, there are still a lot of opportunities out there, particularly in exploration."
Bentley said that the recent agreement with private investors and the Gabonese government to form Energy Africa Gabon had allowed it access to about 90 percent of the country's hydrocarbon basins.
Energy Africa would manage the company, which had six production licences, "and we are in a very good position to look at the opportunities in that country," he said.
Bentley said that Energy Africa planned to drill four exploration and appraisal wells on its existing licences in Africa this year and about 10 in Gabon.
Further exploration opportunities included the Ivory Coast, where it had signed a production sharing agreement with the government in block C1-102.
